content: The study by Fink et al. (2010) was a diagnostic study conducted in Bethesda, Maryland, USA, a non-endemic region for onchocerciasis. The population included 200 patients suspected of having filarial infections, with 129 patients undergoing skin snip microscopy and PCR testing for suspected onchocerciasis. The index test was real-time PCR on skin snips, while the reference test was skin snip microscopy. The study spanned from April 1999 to December 2009. The sensitivity and specificity of skin snip PCR varied between 50% and 88% and 96% to 100%, respectively, depending on the reference standard used. Bayesian methods were employed due to the lack of a gold standard. Boateng et al. (2002) conducted a diagnostic study in Guinea, focusing on two endemic villages, Manikaya and Balan. The study population included 313 individuals, with a community microfilarial load (CMFL) of <1 mf/snippet after 10 years of ivermectin treatment. Skin snip microscopy was used as the reference standard, with a calculated sensitivity of 50% and specificity of 93.8%. The diagnostic odds ratio (DOR) was 15.2, and the positive likelihood ratio (LR+) was 8.1. Pischke et al. (2002) performed a diagnostic study in hyperendemic regions of Western Uganda, where mass drug administration (MDA) had been ongoing since 1991. The study was supported by the German Bundesministerium für Bildung und Forschung and the WHO Special Programme for Tropical Diseases Research. The population included individuals from endemic areas, with skin snip PCR and microscopy used as diagnostic tools. Vincent et al. (2000) studied 38 individuals aged 8–53 years, with 29 undergoing skin snip PCR testing. The study included non-endemic controls to evaluate specificity, which was assumed to be 100%. The study was partially funded by the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases and the Edna McConnell Clark Foundation. Fischer et al. (1996) analyzed 246 individuals, 227 of whom had microfilariae in skin snips before ivermectin treatment. The study did not report a sponsor and focused on the diagnostic performance of skin snip microscopy. Zimmerman et al. (1994) included 191 individuals, with 94 from the Esmeraldas focus in Ecuador. Skin snip microscopy was used as the reference standard, and non-endemic controls were assumed to be microfilariae-negative. The study evaluated the diagnostic performance of skin snip PCR. Golden et al. (2013) conducted a diagnostic study in Burkina Faso and Ivory Coast, analyzing 1,511 individuals from seven villages. The index test was the rapid-format Ov-16 card test (IgG4), with skin snip microscopy as the reference standard. Sensitivity and specificity varied by village, with antibody prevalence correlating with microfilarial prevalence. The study highlighted the impact of control measures on antibody prevalence among individuals born after their implementation. Rodriguez-Perez et al. (2013) evaluated PCR testing in black flies in Chiapas, Mexico. The study included 13,400 flies, with O-150 PCR used as the index test. No significant differences were observed between methods using different pool sizes. Gopal et al. (2012) investigated black flies in Mexico and Burkina Faso, focusing on Simulium ochraceum and Simulium damnosum. The study used O-150 PCR-ELISA for DNA extraction and analysis, with pool sizes up to 200 flies. The study highlighted the cost-effectiveness of oligonucleotide capture assays with increasing pool sizes. Rodriguez-Perez et al. (1999) conducted an entomological survey in Chiapas, Mexico, using O-150 PCR for black fly screening. The study was supported by CONACyT of Mexico. Yameogo et al. (1999) performed a diagnostic study in Ghana, Burkina Faso, and Mali, focusing on areas with long-term vector control. The study evaluated the use of O-150 PCR in black flies to demonstrate the interruption of onchocerciasis transmission in populations receiving MDA.
